title: Filter-aware traversal
summary: Skipping filtered nodes during a graph walk shatters the graph: at 10 percent selectivity on a 16-NN graph the largest reachable component was 11 percent of the passing nodes. It is a percolation threshold that scales as 1/M, and the fix is to traverse everything while collecting only matches.
html:
Day 29 left a gap: predicates too selective for post-filtering and too broad for brute force. The fix is to stop treating the filter as something that happens before or after the search, and evaluate it during the walk.

The obvious way to do that destroys your index, and today is mostly about why.

The obvious way

Walk the graph as usual. When you reach a node that fails the predicate, skip it: do not score it, do not expand it, pretend it is not there. Keep going until you have k matches.

One line of code. It is also wrong, and the failure is structural rather than a matter of degree.

The graph shatters

If you refuse to step on failing nodes, you are not searching your graph any more. You are searching the subgraph induced by the passing nodes, and that subgraph can fall apart.

Measured on a 16-nearest-neighbour graph over 6,500 vectors. For each selectivity I took the passing nodes and asked how much of them a walk could actually reach:

selectivity   passing   largest reachable   fraction
       100%     6,500               6,472      99.6%
        50%     3,250               3,143      96.7%
        25%     1,625               1,357      83.5%
        10%       650                  74      11.4%
         5%       325                   9       2.8%
         1%        65                   2       3.1%

Between 25 percent and 10 percent the graph stops being a graph. At 10 percent selectivity the largest connected group of passing nodes is 74 nodes out of 650, so a perfect search starting from the best possible place can reach at most a ninth of the valid answers. At 5 percent it is nine nodes. Your index has become a pile of fragments.

And this is a recall ceiling nothing downstream can lift. Not a bigger beam, not more probes. The answers are not reachable.

It is percolation, and it is predictable

This is the classic percolation threshold. A node has M neighbours and each survives the filter with probability s, so a passing node keeps about M * s passing neighbours. Below roughly one surviving neighbour per node there is no giant component and the graph is dust.

That predicts the breaking point should scale as 1 / M. It does:

largest reachable fraction, by M and selectivity

                 50%     25%     12%      6%      3%
M=8            83.7%    8.2%    1.6%    2.0%    1.5%
M=16           97.5%   85.2%   16.9%    3.2%    2.6%
M=32           99.6%   97.6%   86.9%   32.3%    7.7%
M=64          100.0%   99.8%   97.7%   85.7%   22.1%

Read the diagonal. Every doubling of M halves the selectivity at which the graph falls apart, exactly as the arithmetic says.

Which gives you a rule worth carrying:

Skipping filtered nodes during traversal is safe only while M * selectivity stays comfortably above about 4. Below that your graph is fragmenting, and your recall ceiling is falling with it.

At the M=16 default from Day 18, that puts the floor at roughly 25 percent selectivity. Most interesting predicates are far more selective than that.

The actual fix

Separate two things the naive version conflated: where you are allowed to walk and what you are allowed to return.

traverse:  every node, filtered or not       keeps the graph connected
collect:   only nodes that pass the filter   keeps the results correct

You route through failing nodes, you score them to decide where to go next, and you simply never put them in the result heap. Connectivity is untouched because the graph you are walking is the full one.

The cost moves rather than disappearing. To collect k matches when a fraction s pass, you visit roughly k / s nodes, which is the same arithmetic as post-filtering. The difference is what the work buys. Post-filtering retrieves a thousand candidates and throws away 990 of them, having paid full distance computation on every one. Filter-aware traversal walks until it has what it needs, so the extra cost is extra hops rather than discarded results, and it cannot come up short the way Day 29's 91 percent did.

On a disk-resident index this distinction matters more, because Day 25 established that a hop is a read. Visiting ten times as many nodes is ten times the I/O, which is why filtered search on DiskANN-style indexes is genuinely hard rather than merely slower.

The other approaches

Partition by filter value. One index per tenant. Perfect recall, trivially correct, and it only works for low cardinality equality filters. A thousand tenants means a thousand indexes to build, warm and keep in memory, and it does nothing for a date range.

Predicate-aware graph construction. Build the graph so that nodes sharing filter values are preferentially connected, which keeps the induced subgraphs connected by design. This is roughly what ACORN and the filtered-DiskANN line of work do. It requires knowing your filter attributes at build time, and it spends edge budget on connectivity you may not need.

Adaptive strategy selection. Estimate selectivity per query, then choose: brute force the survivors when few pass, post-filter when most do, filter-aware traversal in between. This is what mature engines actually ship, and it needs a cardinality estimate, which is the same problem every query planner has had since the 1970s.

What I did not measure

Everything above is about reachability, which is a property of the graph and the filter and is as solid as the arithmetic. I have not measured the recall or latency of the route-through strategy against a real baseline, so take the k / s visit estimate as the straightforward prediction it is rather than something I verified.

I also used random filters throughout. Day 29 showed that real filters are correlated with the data, and a correlated filter should fragment the graph less than a random one of the same selectivity, because surviving nodes are clustered and therefore near each other in the graph. If so, my table is the pessimistic case. That is a measurement worth making on your own data before you trust either version.

Phase 2 ends its vector half here. The next five days are the other tradition, the one that never went away and still beats dense retrieval on exact identifiers. Tomorrow: BM25, and knowing it cold.
exercise:
1. Find your own shattering point. Build a k-NN graph over your embeddings at your real M, then for selectivities of 50, 25, 10 and 5 percent compute the largest connected component among passing nodes. Where it collapses is the selectivity below which naive filter-skipping cannot work for you, whatever your library claims.

2. Check the rule against your config. Take your index's M and your most selective real predicate, and compute M * selectivity. If that number is below about 4, any implementation that skips filtered nodes during traversal has a recall ceiling you cannot tune your way out of. Finding out which strategy your vector database actually uses is worth the twenty minutes of reading its source.

3. Test the correlation question. Repeat exercise 1 twice at the same selectivity, once with a random filter and once with a real one such as a category or tenant. If the real filter fragments less, my table is pessimistic for your workload and you have more headroom than this lesson suggests.
